questions.question: A prompt asks the model to classify sentiment and includes three labeled example reviews before the new review. What technique is this?
options: P-tuning
Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Putting a few input-output demonstrations in the prompt is few-shot (in-context) learning. The model weights do not change. Zero-shot gives no examples, and fine-tuning or p-tuning train parameters.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, Few-Shot Prompting

questions.question: A model keeps getting multi-step arithmetic word problems wrong. Which prompting technique most directly targets this?
options: Removing the system prompt to reduce confusion
Asking for the final answer as a single word, with no reasoning at all
Lowering max_tokens so that the answer is shorter
Chain-of-thought prompting, reasoning step by step first
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps and was shown to improve performance on arithmetic and multi-step reasoning tasks. Forcing very short answers removes the room to reason.

source.title: Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

questions.question: What is zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Giving several worked examples that show their reasoning
Asking the same question several times at temperature 0
Adding "Let's think step by step" with no worked examples
Fine-tuning the model on step-by-step reasoning traces
questions.explanation: Kojima et al. showed that simply appending "Let's think step by step" elicits reasoning without demonstrations. Few-shot CoT, by contrast, includes examples whose reasoning is written out.

source.title: Kojima et al., Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners

questions.question: Self-consistency improves chain-of-thought results by:
options: Asking the model to proofread its answer for spelling errors
Sampling several reasoning paths and taking the majority answer
Running the prompt once at temperature 0 for a stable answer
Fine-tuning the model on its own previous correct answers
questions.explanation: Self-consistency samples multiple diverse chain-of-thought completions (temperature > 0) and takes a majority vote over the final answers. It trades extra inference cost for accuracy.

source.title: Wang et al., Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning

questions.question: Which two statements describe the ReAct prompting pattern? (Select two.)
options: Tool results (Observation) are fed back to guide the next reasoning step
The model updates its own weights with gradient descent after each tool call
Several complete answers are sampled at high temperature and then majority-voted
The model interleaves reasoning steps (Thought) with tool calls (Action)
The model returns only a final answer, keeping all of its intermediate steps hidden
questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions such as search or tool calls, and each observation feeds the next thought. This grounds the reasoning in external information. Majority voting is self-consistency, and no weights are updated at inference.

source.title: Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

questions.question: A developer needs an LLM to return valid JSON matching a schema for every request. Which two practices help most? (Select two.)
options: State the exact schema and give an example of valid output in the prompt
Use the server's structured output or guided JSON decoding feature if available
Ask the model to answer in a friendly, conversational tone with a short greeting
Raise the temperature so the model explores more output formats before settling
Remove all format instructions so the model is not confused by too many rules
questions.explanation: Clear format instructions with an example raise compliance. Constrained (guided) decoding, which many servers including NVIDIA NIM support, restricts tokens so the output follows the schema. Higher temperature increases format errors.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, General Tips for Designing Prompts

questions.question: In a chat-style API, what is the system message typically used for?
options: Storing the replies the assistant generated earlier
Holding only the user's latest question, replacing earlier ones
Logging errors returned by the API server
Setting the assistant's role and rules for the conversation
questions.explanation: The system message sets persistent instructions such as role, tone, constraints and output format. User messages carry the requests, and assistant messages hold previous model replies.

source.title: Hugging Face, Chat templates

questions.question: What is the key difference between prompt engineering and fine-tuning?
options: Fine-tuning works only for images; prompting works only for text
They are synonyms: both change the model in exactly the same way
Prompting changes only the input; fine-tuning updates the weights
Prompting needs GPUs for training; fine-tuning runs without them
questions.explanation: Prompt engineering designs the input (instructions, examples, context) and leaves the weights unchanged. Fine-tuning trains on task data and changes some or all parameters, which costs more but can change behaviour more deeply.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, Prompt Engineering and P-Tuning

questions.question: A few-shot classifier labels almost everything as 'positive'. Its five examples are four positive and one negative. What is the most likely fix?
options: Balance and vary the examples so labels are representative
Remove the instructions and keep only the five examples
Increase max_tokens so the model can explain each label
Switch to beam search with 10 beams for more stable labels
questions.explanation: The label distribution and order of few-shot examples bias the model's predictions. Balanced, representative demonstrations reduce this bias. Output length and beam search don't address the skewed prior.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, Few-Shot Prompting

questions.question: Prompt chaining means:
options: Encrypting each prompt before sending it to the model API
Concatenating all available documents into one huge prompt
Repeating the same prompt again and again until the model agrees with itself
Splitting a task into steps, feeding each output to the next prompt
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining splits a complex task into simpler steps, such as extract, then summarize, then format, with each prompt consuming the previous output. This improves reliability and makes each step easier to debug.

source.title: Prompt Engineering Guide, Prompt Chaining

questions.question: Which two problems does Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) primarily address? (Select two.)
options: Removing the need for a tokenizer before the model
Letting answers cite the source documents they are based on
Updating the model's weights after each user query
Answering from up-to-date or private documents without retraining
Making the model small enough to run on a laptop CPU
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and adds them to the prompt. The model can then use current or proprietary knowledge, and the retrieved chunks give sources to cite. The model's weights don't change and the model is no smaller.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?

questions.question: What is the correct order of a basic RAG query pipeline?
options: Generate an answer, embed the answer, store it, then retrieve it later
Retrieve chunks, retrain the embedding model on them, then generate
Fine-tune the model on the query, then generate the final answer
Embed the query, retrieve similar chunks, add them to the prompt, generate
questions.explanation: At query time RAG embeds the question with the same embedding model used for the documents, runs a similarity search, inserts the top chunks into the prompt as context, and lets the LLM generate a grounded answer.

source.title: Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP

questions.question: Documents were indexed with embedding model A. After an update, queries are embedded with model B. What is the most likely result?
options: Nothing changes, because all embeddings share one space
Retrieval improves automatically because model B is newer
Retrieval breaks: vectors from different models aren't comparable
The vector database converts the old vectors to the new model's space automatically
questions.explanation: Each embedding model defines its own vector space, often with a different dimension. Similarity between vectors from different models is meaningless, so the corpus must be re-embedded whenever the embedding model changes.

source.title: Milvus Docs, Overview

questions.question: A RAG system splits documents into 4,000-token chunks. Answers often include irrelevant information and miss specific facts. What is the most reasonable first experiment?
options: Remove the system prompt to free up context space
Increase the LLM's temperature to explore more answers
Switch the vector index from HNSW to an exact FLAT index
Try smaller chunks with some overlap and measure retrieval
questions.explanation: Very large chunks dilute the embedding with many topics, which hurts retrieval precision and wastes context. Smaller chunks with overlap usually give more focused matches. The right size should be measured on an evaluation set.

source.title: LlamaIndex, Basic strategies: chunk sizes

questions.question: Why do RAG pipelines often add overlap between consecutive chunks?
options: It doubles the index size, which improves recall on its own
Embedding models require duplicated text to work correctly
It makes the LLM generate its answers faster
Ideas that cross a chunk boundary stay intact in one chunk
questions.explanation: Overlap keeps sentences or ideas that cross a boundary intact in at least one chunk, which improves the chance they are retrieved together. The cost is some redundancy in the index.

source.title: LlamaIndex, Basic strategies: chunk sizes

questions.question: Which two statements about rerankers (cross-encoders) in a two-stage retrieval pipeline are correct? (Select two.)
options: They score the query and each candidate together, which is more accurate
They compress the stored vectors so that the index uses much less memory
They generate the final answer that is shown to the user, using the top chunks
They are applied only to the top candidates, because they are too slow for the whole corpus
They split long documents into overlapping chunks before indexing them
questions.explanation: A bi-encoder retrieves candidates quickly from precomputed vectors. A cross-encoder reads the query and each candidate jointly, which is more accurate but expensive, so it only reorders the top-k results from the first stage.

source.title: Sentence Transformers, Retrieve & Re-Rank

questions.question: Users search an internal knowledge base for exact product codes such as 'XG-4471', and pure vector search often misses them. Which two changes help most? (Select two.)
options: Filter or boost on metadata fields such as the product code
Increase the LLM temperature so it considers more candidate products
Use a larger context window and paste the whole catalogue into the prompt
Add keyword search (e.g. BM25) and combine it with vector search (hybrid search)
Replace the embedding model with a smaller one that uses random vectors
questions.explanation: Dense embeddings capture meaning but are weak on exact identifiers. Lexical retrieval such as BM25 matches exact terms, and hybrid search combines both. Metadata filters can also enforce exact matches.

source.title: Milvus Docs, Overview (search types: hybrid, full text BM25, filtering)

questions.question: Which similarity measure compares the direction of two embedding vectors regardless of their length?
options: Cosine similarity
Manhattan distance on token IDs
Hamming distance
Euclidean (L2) distance on raw vectors
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors and ignores magnitude. For normalized vectors, inner product equals cosine similarity, and L2 ranking is equivalent too.

source.title: Milvus Docs, Metric Types

questions.question: When choosing an embedding model for a RAG system over Portuguese legal documents, what is the most reliable way to decide?
options: Evaluate candidates on labeled real queries from the domain
Use the embedding layer of the LLM that will answer
Pick the model with the largest embedding dimension available
Pick the most downloaded model on the model hub
questions.explanation: Public leaderboards are a starting point, but language and domain matter a lot. The reliable method is to measure retrieval metrics such as recall@k or MRR on a small golden set of real queries. Bigger dimensions are not always better and cost more storage.

source.title: NVIDIA DLI, Building RAG Agents with LLMs (course outline)

questions.question: What does an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index such as HNSW trade off?
options: Faster LLM training in exchange for slower inference
A small loss in recall for much faster search
Shorter documents in exchange for lower cost
Exact results in exchange for slower search
questions.explanation: ANN indexes avoid comparing the query with every vector, so search is much faster, but they may miss some true nearest neighbours. FLAT (brute force) is the only index that guarantees exact results.

source.title: Milvus Docs, Index Explained

questions.question: HNSW indexes are built as:
options: A hash table of vectors, keyed by their token IDs
A binary tree of vectors, sorted by their vector norm
A layered proximity graph, searched from a coarse top layer down
A list of cluster centroids, searched by visiting nprobe clusters
questions.explanation: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds layered graphs. Search enters at the sparse top layer and descends, refining the nearest neighbours. Searching cluster centroids with nprobe describes IVF indexes.

source.title: Malkov & Yashunin, Efficient and robust ANN search using HNSW graphs

questions.question: An IVF index returns too many poor matches. Without rebuilding, which search parameter most directly increases recall (at some cost in latency)?
options: Reduce top-k so fewer results are returned
Lower the embedding dimension of the query vectors
Increase nprobe, the number of clusters searched
Decrease nlist to 1 at query time
questions.explanation: IVF partitions vectors into nlist clusters and at query time searches only the nprobe closest clusters. Raising nprobe searches more clusters, which improves recall but takes longer. nlist is fixed when the index is built.

source.title: Milvus Docs, In-memory Index (IVF_FLAT parameters)

questions.question: A team has 500 million embeddings and limited RAM. Which two index types reduce memory by compressing the stored vectors? (Select two.)
options: IVF_PQ (product quantization)
IVF_FLAT
IVF_SQ8 (scalar quantization to 8-bit)
A plain Python list of vectors
FLAT
questions.explanation: Product quantization encodes sub-vectors with small codebooks, and SQ8 turns each 4-byte float into 1 byte. Both cut memory sharply at some cost in recall. FLAT and IVF_FLAT store full uncompressed vectors.

source.title: Milvus Docs, Index Explained

questions.question: A developer wants a local, in-process library for fast similarity search in a prototype, with no server to run. Which option fits best?
options: A managed cloud vector database
Triton Inference Server
FAISS
A relational database without vector support
questions.explanation: FAISS is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors that runs in-process, on CPU or GPU. Managed services need network setup, and Triton serves models, not vector search.

source.title: FAISS wiki

questions.question: Why are sentence-embedding models such as Sentence-BERT preferred over raw BERT [CLS] outputs for semantic search?
options: They work directly on characters, with no tokenizer
They generate text as well as embeddings
They are trained so cosine similarity reflects meaning
They have no maximum input sequence length
questions.explanation: Sentence-BERT fine-tunes BERT with siamese networks so that sentence vectors can be compared directly with cosine similarity. Raw BERT embeddings perform poorly for this and need a cross-encoder for every pair.

source.title: Reimers & Gurevych, Sentence-BERT

questions.question: A RAG chatbot answers "What about the second one?" poorly because retrieval uses only the latest message. What is a standard fix?
options: Raise the temperature for follow-up questions
Increase the chunk size so each chunk covers whole documents
Rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question first
Disable retrieval for every follow-up question
questions.explanation: Conversational RAG often uses an LLM to condense the history and the follow-up into a standalone query, so the retriever receives a self-contained question. Without it, pronouns like 'the second one' carry no meaning for the search.

source.title: LangChain Docs, Retrieval

questions.question: A company wants an assistant that answers from internal policies, which change weekly, and must cite the source document. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Fine-tuning every week is the cheapest way to keep the answers current
Fine-tuning guarantees that the model can cite the exact source document
RAG makes citations easy because the retrieved chunks carry document metadata
Prompting alone can add new policies without them ever appearing in the prompt
RAG fits because documents can be re-indexed when they change, without retraining the model
questions.explanation: RAG keeps knowledge outside the weights, so updates only need re-indexing, and the retrieved chunks carry metadata for citation. Weekly fine-tuning is expensive and doesn't provide source attribution.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?

questions.question: word2vec learns word vectors by:
options: Asking an LLM to write a description of every word
Training a shallow network to predict words from their context
Counting how often each character appears in each word of the corpus
Assigning each word a random vector that never changes
questions.explanation: word2vec (CBOW and skip-gram) trains a shallow network on context prediction. The learned vectors place words used in similar contexts close together, so vector arithmetic can capture analogies.

source.title: Mikolov et al., Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

questions.question: What is a key limitation of static word embeddings (e.g. word2vec) compared with contextual embeddings from Transformers?
options: They can only represent images, not words
They require a GPU to look up a vector
Each word gets one vector, whatever its context
They cannot be saved to disk after training
questions.explanation: Static embeddings assign one vector per word type. Contextual models such as BERT produce a different representation for each occurrence depending on the surrounding words, which resolves ambiguity.

source.title: Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (Ch. 6 and 11)

questions.question: In a RAG pipeline, which component turns documents and queries into vectors?
options: The vector database's query planner
The embedding model
The reranker
The LLM's output layer
questions.explanation: The embedding model encodes text into dense vectors. The vector database stores and searches those vectors, and the LLM generates the answer. All three are separate components.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
